1: # APA Redline — Brightline Cabinetry asset sale (seller side)
2: 
3: Buyer's draft: Lone Star Millwork Holdings LLC "standard form," received with cover email from J. Whitaker.
4: Sections redlined per engagement scope: §§2.4, 3.3, 4.12, 7.4(a)–(c), 8.2, 9.3.
5: 
6: **Price inference used throughout:** price is not stated anywhere in the client file; escrow is "$310,000 (10%)" (§9.3) ⇒ $310,000 ÷ 0.10 = **$3,100,000**. Treat as inferred, and confirm against §2.1 of the full APA (not provided).
7: **Citations:** all authorities are from `library/INDEX.md`, cited as `library/<file>.md`.
8: 
9: ---
10: 
11: ## Assumption and arithmetic block (shown, per the working rules)
12: 
13: 1. Implied price = 310,000 / 0.10 = **$3,100,000**. General-rep cap = 10% × 3,100,000 = **$310,000** (equals escrow). Basket = 75,000 / 3,100,000 = **2.42%** of price.
14: 2. Installer exposure (upper the buyer will calculate):
15:    - Employer FICA at 7.65% (upper-bound payroll figure; **not stated in the library — verify**; library notes IRC §3509 reduced rates if non-willful): 612,000 × 7.65% = **$46,818/yr**; × 3.4-yr average tenure = **$159,181**.
16:    - Overtime premium, half-time extra on hours over 40 (method is standard payroll arithmetic, **not stated in the library — verify**): rate midpoint (34+41)/2 = $37.50 ⇒ $18.75 per OT hour.
17:      - Scenario A (Ray: 45–50 hrs/wk in busy season; length unknown — **assumed 12 weeks**): 10 OT-hrs/wk × 12 wks = 120 OT-hrs/yr ⇒ 18.75 × 120 × 9 workers = **$20,250/yr** ⇒ × 3.4 yrs = **$68,850**.
18:      - Scenario B, conservative (buyer's likely model, 45 hrs all year): 5 × 50 = 250 OT-hrs/yr ⇒ 18.75 × 250 × 9 = **$42,188/yr** ⇒ × 3.4 yrs = **$143,438**.
19:    - Bracketed indicative total: **$228,031 (7.4% of price) to $302,619 (9.8% of price)** vs. escrow of $310,000. Prior-year 1099 totals were not provided (client answered no additional info); 2025 is used as the annual run-rate proxy. The FLSA recovery period is **not in the library**, so 3.4 years (census average tenure) is used as the exposure window rather than a limitations-based period.
20: 3. Earn-out gate arithmetic: full $400,000 requires EBITDA of 700,000 + 400,000/0.40 = **$1,700,000**. Clean 2025 EBITDA = 740,000 − 180,000 − 42,000 = **$518,000**; with a replacement manager at Ray's comp: 518,000 − 180,000 = **$338,000**. Buyer-measured post-closing: earn-out **$0** in both cases; even unchanged seller-prepared basis yields 0.40 × (740,000 − 700,000) = **$16,000**.
21: 4. WARN: 14 W-2 employees; even adding the 9 installers as employees = 23, under the 100-employee threshold.
22: 
23: ---
24: 
25: ## §2.4 Earn-Out — **CHANGE**
26: 
27: **Buyer's draft (as received):** 40% of EBITDA (12 months post-closing) above $700,000, max $400,000; "EBITDA" determined by Buyer in good faith under Buyer's accounting policies, consistently applied.
28: 
29: **Replacement language:**
30: 
31: > "§2.4 Earn-Out. In addition to the Closing Payment, Buyer shall pay Seller 40% of the excess of EBITDA of the Business for the twelve (12) months following Closing over $700,000, up to a maximum Earn-Out payment of $400,000.
32: > (a) 'EBITDA' means earnings of the Business before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, determined in accordance with GAAP, consistently applied, and consistent with the Seller's historical accounting practices reflected in the 2025 financial statements, provided that:
33: >   (i) there shall be added back owner's compensation for the pre-Closing period, offset by a deduction for compensation actually paid by Buyer to operate the Business in lieu of owner compensation (up to $180,000 per annum);
34: >   (ii) non-recurring legal fees of $42,000 incurred pre-Closing are excluded;
35: >   (iii) there shall be excluded any corporate overhead, management fees, allocation charges, transaction, integration or purchase-accounting costs attributable to Buyer or its Affiliates; and
36: >   (iv) no charge shall reduce EBITDA to the extent attributable to changes Buyer makes to pricing or contract terms contrary to pre-Closing practice.
37: > (b) Buyer shall operate the Business in the ordinary course consistent with past practice. If Buyer fails to do so with the purpose of avoiding or delaying payment, EBITDA shall be calculated as if Buyer had so operated.
38: > (c) Buyer shall deliver quarterly statements of EBITDA with supporting detail; Seller may audit Buyer's calculation on reasonable notice; disputes resolved by an independent accountant whose fees Buyer bears unless Seller's error exceeds 5%.
39: > (d) If Buyer sells the Business or substantially all its assets during the Earn-Out period, the unpaid Earn-Out accelerates, calculated on EBITDA through the closing date of such sale annualized."

41: **Why:** "EBITDA as determined by Buyer under Buyer's policies" is the classic buyer-control formulation that lets overhead allocations, management fees, integration costs and purchase-accounting adjustments zero the earn-out; seller protections are exactly the set in `library/earnout_definitions.md` (*Lazard Technology Partners v. Qinetiq*, 114 A.3d 193 (Del. 2015)). If buyer refuses the definition, the fallback is negotiation of the gate toward achievable EBITDA or payment in cash/holdback instead.

44: 
45: **Buyer's draft:** "Seller shall use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain the consents listed on Schedule 3.3 prior to Closing. (Schedule 3.3, as drafted by Buyer: 'None.')"
46: 
47: **Replacement language:**
48: 
49: > "§3.3 Required Consents. Seller shall use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain, prior to Closing, the consents listed on **Schedule 3.3 (Required Consents)**, and Buyer shall cooperate. Failure to obtain a consent listed on Schedule 3.3 shall not excuse Buyer from Closing provided Seller has used commercially reasonable efforts, except in the case of the Hensley Homes Master Supply Agreement consent, which shall be a condition precedent to Closing. Seller and Buyer shall cooperate on the reapplication process described on Schedule 3.3 for the spray-booth permit."

Strategy and facts (consent not sought; owner unaware) from the client's answer to question 1: a personal approach from Ray is the highest-probability path and should happen **before signing**. Schedule 4.12 lists the nine (9) individuals who have been treated as independent contractors ("Installers") during the three (3) years prior to the date hereof; except as set forth on Schedule 4.12, Seller represents that all individuals providing services to the Business have been properly classified as employees or independent contractors under applicable law and that Seller has withheld and paid all required taxes."

Oracle*; Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§317, 322, per our referenced authority, `library/anti_assignment_change_of_control.md`).

23: ## 2. WARN
24: 
25: Confirmed **no WARN exposure** on this headcount, and the reason is structural rather than a close call:
26: 
27: - WARN reaches employers with **100 or more employees** (excluding part-time) and covers plant closings/mass layoffs affecting 50+ employees at a single site (29 U.S.C. §2101(a)(1) as summarized in `library/warn_act.md`; primary/affiliates exclusion in 20 C.F.R. §639.3).

30: - Texas has no mini-WARN statute; the county-based state analog is likewise not a factor at this headcount.
31: 
32: So your client may proceed on its planned staffing decisions free of WARN notice obligations for this target. Fresenius* (Del. Ch. 2018) (dicta)).

28: - The Brightline census shows **14 W-2 employees** (7 shop, 4 installers, 3 office), no union, single site.
29: - Even if your client elects to treat the 9 "independent installers" as employees for WARN counting (readers of our correspondence will see that classification is separately addressed on the disclosure side), the count is 14 + 9 = **23 — well under 100**. A business this size is not a covered employer, and there is no WARN duty even if Buyer ultimately hires fewer than all of them.
30: - Texas has no mini-WARN statute; the county-based state analog is likewise not a factor at this headcount.
31: 
32: So your client may proceed on its planned staffing decisions free of WARN notice obligations for this target. (We note for completeness only: nothing here should be confused with the *other* heads of exposure around the installers — decoupled from WARN, those are addressed in ¶3 and the indemnity scheduling.)

36: We cannot accept §7.4(c) as drafted ("knowledge acquired (or capable of being acquired) at any time, whether before or after the execution of this Agreement"). Our authority on practice confirms the alternative approaches; a seller who discloses a known item and then signs a clean rep under a pro-sandbagging clause has simply pre-paid an indemnity for that item, which is not anyone's intent here (`library/sandbagging.md`, citing Delaware/Texas practice and *Akorn v. Fresenius* (Del. Ch. 2018) (dicta)).

46:

48: 
49: Regards,
50: Counsel for Brightline Cabinetry LLC

54: ## Addendum — response to "§7.4(c) is market, every deal has it" and "§4.12 is a plain-vanilla compliance rep"

58: ### 1. "Is market, every deal has it"
59: 
60: Two points, without heat:
61: 
62: - **On market practice:** the authorities we rely on treat this as a live choice, not a universal: both pro-sandbagging and anti-sandbagging provisions are described as market alternatives (`library/sandbagging.md`, citing ABA Private Target Deal Points Study). We do not need to win the philosophy fight — see the package below, which lets Buyer keep the clause.
63: - **On the particular wording:** even the aggressive form our authority describes turns on buyer knowledge *before signing or closing*. Your draft — knowledge "acquired (or capable of being acquired) **at any time**, whether before or after the execution of this Agreement" — reaches matters discovered after execution, which goes beyond the formulation we find described. Whatever is "market" for pre-signing knowledge is not necessarily market for that open-ended extension, and we are not persuaded it is common.
64: 
65: ### 2. "§4.12 is vanilla — if Ray's contractors are fine, what's the concern?"
66: 
67: We agree the rep is vanilla. The premise is not. Buyer's own diligence file (data room §2.2) says the nine "independent installers": work exclusively for Brightline, drive Brightline trucks, use shop tools, are scheduled daily by the shop foreman, are paid hourly ($34–41), and average ~3.4 years of tenure, at 45–50 hours in busy season paid straight time. 76: **The one combination we cannot sign into the clean rep:** a rep we know is false + no schedule + full-price cap + post-signing knowledge coverage. On your draft exactly as received, our advice to our client will be not to sign — and we would rather close the deal than grandstand over it, which is why Option B asks you to give up almost nothing you have said you need.

6: **Pro-sandbagging** clause: buyer may recover for breach of a representation even if it knew of the inaccuracy before signing/closing. **Anti-sandbagging**: buyer may not recover for breaches it knew of. Sellers who disclose a known issue (e.g., contractor classification) in diligence and then give a clean representation subject to a pro-sandbagging clause have effectively agreed to indemnify for the disclosed issue. 1: # Note to Ray — the plain-English version
2: 
3: Ray —
4: 
5: You said "just tell me what bites me later." Here are the three things that cost you money **after** closing, worst first. Nothing below is a lawyer trick; it's arithmetic and contract text in the buyer's own draft.
6: 
7: ## 1. Your installers — this is the one that bites (and buyer will make you pay for it twice)
8: 
9: You told me "everyone in the industry does it" and "they like it." Both are true and both are irrelevant. The legal test looks at who controls the work, not the 1099 form. Nine men working only for Brightline, in your trucks, with your tools, scheduled every day by your foreman, paid hourly for 3–4 years: **the law calls them employees no matter what the 1099s say** (that's the IRS finding structure with the control factors — see `library/worker_classification_tx_irs.md`, IRS Rev. Rul. 87-41).
10: 
11: What it costs (shown arithmetic; the flagged assumptions are in the redline):
12: 
13: - Employer payroll taxes on their pay: $612,000 (2025) × 7.65% = **$46,818/yr**; over their ~3.4-year average tenure ≈ **$159,181**. (The 7.65% employer-share figure is a common payroll number but is not stated in the reference library, so treat it as an unverified upper-bound assumption. The library does note that the reduced-rate regime under IRC §3509 applies only where the failure is *not* willful — see `library/worker_classification_tx_irs.md`.)
14: - Overtime on straight-hourly pay when they're at 45–50 hours: at a $37.50/hr midpoint wage, add ~$18.75 for every hour over 40. Your busy season alone: 9 installers × 10 OT hrs/wk × ~$18.75 × 12 weeks = **$20,250/yr** (busy-season length not in your records — my assumption). Buyer's diligence model will assume more, up to ~**$143,438** total if it assumes 45 hours all year.
15: - **Bracket: $228,000–$303,000** — which is 7–10% of your price and nearly your whole $310,000 escrow.
16: 
17: And here's the part that actually costs extra: **you signed a "clean" rep** (§4.12) saying everyone is properly classified and all taxes were paid. That isn't true. Buyer's §7.4(c) says they can collect even on things they knew about — before or after signing. Put together, you have promised to insure Lone Star for a problem they knew was in the room. My fix (in the redline): disclose the installers up front and replace the blank check with a **capped special indemnity of $275,000**. That's what it costs to stop the bleeding; uncapped, the clause as written reaches the entire price.
18: 
19: ## 2. The earn-out — as written, it's worth about zero. Don't price it into your "sell number"
20: 
21: Buyer agreed to pay you 40% of EBITDA above $700,000, capped at $400,000. Sounds good. Watch the math:
22: 
23: | | Amount |
24: |---|---|
25: | Earn full earn-out requires EBITDA of | 700,000 + 400,000 ÷ 0.40 = **$1,700,000** (2.3× your 2025 figure) |
26: | Your 2025 EBITDA per your own numbers | $740,000 — but that counts your $180k salary and $42k "one-time" legal **as add-backs** |
27: | Same business without those add-backs | 740 − 180 − 42 = **$518,000** |
28: | If buyer pays a manager ~$180k to run it | 518 − 180 = **$338,000** |
29: | Either way vs. the $700,000 gate | **below the gate → you get $0** |
30: | Even in best case (your numbers unchanged) | 0.40 × (740 − 700k) = **$16,000** |
31: 
32: The killer isn't the gate — it's the words: "EBITDA ... **as determined by Buyer** in accordance with **Buyer's accounting policies**." Buyer writes both the score and the rules; provisions like that are the textbook mechanism buyers use to pay efficiently nothing post-closing (`library/earnout_definitions.md`). My redline fixes the definition, adds audit rights and acceleration if they flip the business. **Until it's fixed, treat the earn-out as worth $0 when you're deciding whether the $3.1M cash offer is enough.**
33: 
34: ## 3. Hensley Homes — your biggest customer can say "no," and you haven't asked yet
35: 
36: Hensley is 38% of your revenue — about $1.75M/year. Their contract says you **cannot transfer it without their written consent**, they can refuse **for any reason or no reason** ("sole discretion" — that's in the data room, §1.1), and a transfer made anyway is void. You told me he's a friend, he doesn't know yet, and he "won't love a corporate buyer." Right now the plan per buyer's schedule is "no consents needed" — which is false.
37: 
38: Two things to do: (1) **tell him yourself, before you sign anything** — this is the classic moment where a friend finds out from a letterhead instead of from you; and (2) tell him the shop keeps running as it always has, which is the pitch for the consent letter. If he says no or wants something for it, better to know **before** you're bound to close. My redline makes his consent a closing condition so you're not trapped.
39: 
40: Two smaller ones while I have you: the **spray-booth permit** doesn't transfer — the city makes the buyer reapply, 30–60 days — so the real closing date is 30–60 days after signing, not two weeks. And the **non-compete** as drafted is 7 years within 500 miles — you'd sign it, you're retiring, but I've cut it to 3 years / 75 miles because courts dislike overbroad ones and a bloated one invites tax scrutiny if they shove purchase price into it (see `library/tx_noncompete_sale_of_business.md`).
41:

1: # Reply to Buyer's Counsel — Brightline Cabinetry asset sale
2: 
3: **To:** J. Whitaker (Lone Star Millwork Holdings LLC)
4: **From:** Counsel for Ray Brightline / Brightline Cabinetry LLC
5: **Re:** APA draft — Schedule 3.3, WARN, and §7.4(c)
6: 
7: Whitaker —
8: 
9: Thanks for the draft and the two questions. Answers below, plus one correction to a premise.
10: 
11: ## 1. Schedule 3.3 / consents
12: 
13: We do not share the premise that "there are no consent issues," and we cannot accept Schedule 3.3 in its drafted form ("None"). On this record:
14: 
15: - **Hensley Homes Master Supply Agreement** — Brightline's largest customer (38% of revenue, i.e., $1,748,000 of the $4.6M 2025 figure shown in the data room). Its §18 bars assignment "by operation of law, merger, sale of assets, change of control or otherwise" without prior written consent, consent may be withheld **in Hensley's sole discretion**, and a non-consensual assignment is void. In an asset sale delivering these contracts, a clause of that breadth is enforced according to its terms, and the transfer without consent is a breach and void where the clause so provides (*SQL Solutions v. Oracle*; Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§317, 322, per our referenced authority, `library/anti_assignment_change_of_control.md`).
16: - **Shop lease, 7700 Burleson Rd (through 2029), §22** — landlord consent required, "not unreasonably withheld."
17: - **City of Austin spray-booth permit** — issued to the LLC, non-transferable; the new owner must reapply, and the city's processing runs **30–60 days**. This one is a closing-calendar item as well as a consent schedule item.
18: - **Cascade Builders framework agreement (11%)** — assignment to a successor to substantially all assets is permitted on notice; included for completeness as a notice item, not a consent.
19: - **Twenty-two residential contracts (<$40k each)** — silent on assignment; no consent changes needed on the authority we rely on (contract rights assignable absent language to the contrary; obligations require consent only if personal performance has been made a condition — see `library/anti_assignment_change_of_control.md`). Flagged for completeness; buyer assuming the obligations at closing addresses interpersonal concerns.
20: 
21: **ACTION — Seller will deliver a marked Schedule 3.3 reflecting the five items above and will propose that the APA make Hensley's consent (or an agreed accommodation with Hensley) a condition to Closing, with a drop-dead date.** As you'd expect with a sole-discretion consent standard, our client is speaking with Hensley's principal directly; this is a personal relationship and we'd ask that your client not approach Hensley unilaterally while we do that. Separately: your Schedule 3.1(c) ("Assigned Contracts") was not included in the materials we received; please send it so we can confirm the schedules line up with your list.
22: 
23: ## 2. WARN
24: 
25: Confirmed **no WARN exposure** on this headcount, and the reason is structural rather than a close call:
26: 
27: - WARN reaches employers with **100 or more employees** (excluding part-time) and covers plant closings/mass layoffs affecting 50+ employees at a single site (29 U.S.C. §2101(a)(1) as summarized in `library/warn_act.md`; primary/affiliates exclusion in 20 C.F.R. §639.3).
28: - The Brightline census shows **14 W-2 employees** (7 shop, 4 installers, 3 office), no union, single site.
29: - Even if your client elects to treat the 9 "independent installers" as employees for WARN counting (readers of our correspondence will see that classification is separately addressed on the disclosure side), the count is 14 + 9 = **23 — well under 100**. A business this size is not a covered employer, and there is no WARN duty even if Buyer ultimately hires fewer than all of them.
30: - Texas has no mini-WARN statute; the county-based state analog is likewise not a factor at this headcount.
31: 
32: So your client may proceed on its planned staffing decisions free of WARN notice obligations for this target. (We note for completeness only: nothing here should be confused with the *other* heads of exposure around the installers — decoupled from WARN, those are addressed in ¶3 and the indemnity scheduling.)
33: 
34: ## 3. §7.4(c) — our position
35: 
36: We cannot accept §7.4(c) as drafted ("knowledge acquired (or capable of being acquired) at any time, whether before or after the execution of this Agreement"). That is the broadest pro-sandbagging formulation, and it is not a reasonable simplification **in this transaction**: it operates together with other provisions of your draft to make Seller the insurer of any issue Buyer learns about anywhere, any time — including on the §4.12 classification facts we are scheduling. Our authority on practice confirms the alternative approaches; a seller who discloses a known item and then signs a clean rep under a pro-sandbagging clause has simply pre-paid an indemnity for that item, which is not anyone's intent here (`library/sandbagging.md`, citing Delaware/Texas practice and *Akorn v. Fresenius* (Del. Ch. 2018) (dicta)).
37:

Separately: your Schedule 3.1(c) ("Assigned Contracts") was not included in the materials we received; please send it so we can confirm the schedules line up with your list.
22: 
23: ## 2. WARN

25: Confirmed **no WARN exposure** on this headcount, and the reason is structural rather than a close call:
26: 
27: - WARN reaches employers with **100 or more employees** (excluding part-time) and covers plant closings/mass layoffs affecting 50+ employees at a single site (29 U.S.C. §2101(a)(1) as summarized in `library/warn_act.md`; primary/affiliates exclusion in 20 C.F.R. §639.3).
28: - The Brightline census shows **14 W-2 employees** (7 shop, 4 installers, 3 office), no union, single site.
29: - Even if your client elects to treat the 9 "independent installers" as employees for WARN counting (readers of our correspondence will see that classification is separately addressed on the disclosure side), the count is 14 + 9 = **23 — well under 100**. 30: - Texas has no mini-WARN statute; the county-based state analog is likewise not a factor at this headcount.
31: 
32: So your client may proceed on its planned staffing decisions free of WARN notice obligations for this target. (We note for completeness only: nothing here should be confused with the *other* heads of exposure around the installers — decoupled from WARN, those are addressed in ¶3 and the indemnity scheduling.)
33:

35: 
36: We cannot accept §7.4(c) as drafted ("knowledge acquired (or capable of being acquired) at any time, whether before or after the execution of this Agreement"). That is the broadest pro-sandbagging formulation, and it is not a reasonable simplification **in this transaction**: it operates together with other provisions of your draft to make Seller the insurer of any issue Buyer learns about anywhere, any time — including on the §4.12 classification facts we are scheduling. Our authority on practice confirms the alternative approaches; a seller who discloses a known item and then signs a clean rep under a pro-sandbagging clause has simply pre-paid an indemnity for that item, which is not anyone's intent here (`library/sandbagging.md`, citing Delaware/Texas practice and *Akorn v. Fresenius* (Del. Ch. 2018) (dicta)).
37: 
38: Our counter is attached as a redline; in substance:
39: 
40: - **§7.4(c)** becomes an anti-sandbagging provision: Buyer's recovery is not affected by Buyer's knowledge, but is precluded (outside Fundamental Representations and Buyer's knowing fraud, and outside scheduled matters, where recovery runs through the newly-added §7.1A Special Indemnity) where Buyer had actual knowledge of the breach at or prior to Closing.

A capped special indemnity is the market-typical answer where a buyer wants certainty on a specific known item; a full-price-cap rep with statute-of-limitations-plus survival for an operational matter like this is not the market answer (`library/baskets_caps.md`).
42: - **§7.4(b)**: we pull §4.12 back under the general 10% cap, and cap the classification exposure specifically through §7.1A. Buyer keeps Fundamental Reps at full price cap. Nothing above touches Buyer's fraud or Buyer's right to be told the truth through schedules.
43: - Closing mechanics note (not a numbered section): the spray-booth reapplication window (30–60 days) is on everyone's critical path. Signing in two weeks works if Buyer is flexible on the closing date; we'd propose a target closing of approximately 60 days post-signing.

54: ## Addendum — response to "§7.4(c) is market, every deal has it" and "§4.12 is a plain-vanilla compliance rep"
55: 
56: Received via our client; responding on the merits.
57: 
58: ### 1. "Is market, every deal has it"
59: 
60: Two points, without heat:
61: 
62: - **On market practice:** the authorities we rely on treat this as a live choice, not a universal: both pro-sandbagging and anti-sandbagging provisions are described as market alternatives (`library/sandbagging.md`, citing ABA Private Target Deal Points Study). We do not need to win the philosophy fight — see the package below, which lets Buyer keep the clause.
63: - **On the particular wording:** even the aggressive form our authority describes turns on buyer knowledge *before signing or closing*. Your draft — knowledge "acquired (or capable of being acquired) **at any time**, whether before or after the execution of this Agreement" — reaches matters discovered after execution, which goes beyond the formulation we find described. Whatever is "market" for pre-signing knowledge is not necessarily market for that open-ended extension, and we are not persuaded it is common.
64: 
65: ### 2. "§4.12 is vanilla — if Ray's contractors are fine, what's the concern?"
66: 
67: We agree the rep is vanilla. The premise is not. Buyer's own diligence file (data room §2.2) says the nine "independent installers": work exclusively for Brightline, drive Brightline trucks, use shop tools, are scheduled daily by the shop foreman, are paid hourly ($34–41), and average ~3.4 years of tenure, at 45–50 hours in busy season paid straight time. Under the common-law control test, that census describes employees, not contractors, and the same authority expressly notes "industry practice" is no defense (`library/worker_classification_tx_irs.md`, IRS Rev. Rul. 87-41; Treas. Reg. §31.3121(d)-1).
68: 
69: So the concern is concrete: as drafted, §4.12 is a knowingly false statement, §7.4(b) caps it at the full Purchase Price, and §7.4(c) preserves the claim even though Buyer knows the facts. Indicative arithmetic (assumptions flagged in our redline): employer FICA at an upper-bound 7.65% on $612,000 of annual installer pay = $46,818/yr; overtime premiums $20,250–$42,188/yr; both over 3.4-year average tenure → indicative bracket **$228,031–$302,619**. Signing the clean rep turns that into exposure up to the full price, far beyond the $310,000 escrow. Vanilla practice — and both sides' deal points studies say the same — is that a known issue goes on the schedule or gets a sized special indemnity (`library/sandbagging.md` (seller protections (ii)–(iii)); `library/baskets_caps.md`: "a specific operational rep (like worker classification) carved out to a full-price cap is off-market and should be resisted or replaced with a sized special indemnity").

71: ### 3. The pragmatic package — either option gets this signed
72: 
73: - **Option A (our redline, prior letter):** anti-sandbagging §7.4(c) with Fundamental-Rep and fraud carve-outs; classification boxed by Schedule 4.12 + §7.1A ($275,000 cap); §4.12 off the full-price carve-out.
74: - **Option B (concession, offered here):** Buyer keeps its §7.4(c) **verbatim** for every unscheduled matter, and the deal adds only: (i) the new **Schedule 4.12** listing the nine installers; (ii) the **§7.1A Special Indemnity capped at $275,000** as Buyer's exclusive remedy for the scheduled classification matters (buyer's knowing fraud and Fundamental-Rep breaches excepted); and (iii) §4.12 removed from the §7.4(b) full-price carve-out. Net effect: Buyer keeps its "market" clause intact for everything else; the one known item is priced and capped — $275,000, ~8.9% of the inferred $3.1M price, inside the $310,000 escrow — and the seller is not reciting a falsehood he will pay for at the buyer's option.
75: 
76: **The one combination we cannot sign into the clean rep:** a rep we know is false + no schedule + full-price cap + post-signing knowledge coverage. On your draft exactly as received, our advice to our client will be not to sign — and we would rather close the deal than grandstand over it, which is why Option B asks you to give up almost nothing you have said you need.
77: 
78: Mechanics unchanged from our prior letter: the Schedule 3.3 counter is ready to deliver; your Schedule 3.1(c) remains outstanding; and the spray-booth reapplication (30–60 days) sets the closing calendar whatever we do at signing. If the package is agreed, signing next week is realistic.
